metadata.title: How the Center of America Moved West
metadata.section: Section D: Demographics, Real Estate & Urban Drift
metadata.visual_form: Animated Map with Moving Center Point
metadata.data_notes: Census measures the center once every 10 years (1790-2020). Years in between are a straight-line fill.

events.label: First census: center in Kent County, Maryland
Biggest westward jump: about 80 miles in a decade
Center near Hartville, Missouri (877 miles west)

explanation.summary: Imagine the United States as a flat board with every person the same weight. The point where the board would balance is the "center of population." In 1790 it was near Baltimore. Over 230 years it moved 877 miles west and 128 miles south, to the Missouri Ozarks.
explanation.methodology: Mean center of population for each census, 1790-2020, from Table 1 of the Census Bureau's 2020 Centers of Population documentation. Miles west and south are measured from the 1790 point. The Census measures the center only once every 10 years; years in between are a straight line.

key_findings.title: 1850s: The Biggest Leap West
key_findings.description: Between 1850 and 1860 the center moved about 80 miles west, the largest jump of any decade, as settlers poured into the Midwest and California.
key_findings.significance: The fastest westward shift in the nation's history.

key_findings.title: 1980: Across the Mississippi
key_findings.description: For the first time, the center crossed the Mississippi River into Missouri (Jefferson County).
key_findings.significance: From 1950 on, the center also moved steadily south as the Sun Belt grew.

key_findings.title: 2020: Wright County, Missouri
key_findings.description: The 2020 center is near Hartville, Missouri, 877 miles west and 128 miles south of the 1790 point. Since 1950 the center has moved about 96 miles south, three times as far as in the 160 years before.
key_findings.significance: America's growth has shifted from the West to the South and Southwest.
